description: Judgement, influence and delivery skills for a cloud/platform architect: cognitive biases and forecasting, systems thinking and org behaviour, persuasion and negotiation, decision writing (ADRs, memos), speaking, facilitation, product thinking and learning science.

notes.front: Kahneman: what distinguishes System 1 from System 2 thinking?
notes.back:
System 1: fast, automatic, effortless, always on.
System 2: slow, deliberate, effortful, and lazy: it endorses System 1's answer unless forced to engage.
notes.analogy: System 1 is the autopilot; System 2 is the pilot who only takes the controls when an alarm sounds.
notes.extra: In practice: To get a System 2 decision from a chief technology officer (CTO), send a one-page options memo with numbers before the meeting so the deliberate work is cheap.

notes.front: What is the anchoring effect, and what is the defence against it?
notes.back:
Estimates are pulled toward the first number seen, even an irrelevant one.
Defence: form your own estimate first, and deliberately consider a counter-anchor.
notes.extra: In practice: Vendor list prices exist mainly as anchors. Open with a peer benchmark or competing quote, and state your recommended number to the chief financial officer (CFO) first.

notes.front: What is the availability heuristic?
notes.back: Judging frequency or probability by how easily examples come to mind. Recent, vivid or emotional events feel more likely than they are.
notes.extra: In practice: After one public cloud outage a board overweights cloud risk and ignores the on-prem array that fails twice a year. Counter with base rates: 24 months of incidents by cause.

notes.front: What is base rate neglect?
notes.back: Ignoring the prior probability of an outcome in favour of case-specific details that feel diagnostic.
notes.extra: In practice: 'This startup vendor has a great demo.' Base rate: most infrastructure startups are acquired or fold within five years. Ask for the base rate before judging the demo.

notes.front: What is confirmation bias, and what is a structural counter-measure?
notes.back:
Seeking and interpreting evidence to support what you already believe.
Counter: define disconfirming evidence in advance, and assign someone to argue the opposite (red team).
notes.extra: In practice: A Proof of Concept (PoC) run by the team that chose the tool will 'succeed'. Set pass/fail criteria before it starts and have another team evaluate.

notes.front: What is hindsight bias, and how does it damage post-incident reviews?
notes.back: Once the outcome is known it seems to have been predictable. Reasonable decisions under uncertainty get recast as 'obvious mistakes', which drives blame.
notes.extra: In practice: Reconstruct what was known at each decision point: 'Given the information at 14:02, the rollback decision was correct.'

notes.front: What does WYSIATI mean, and why does it inflate confidence?
notes.back: 'What You See Is All There Is': System 1 builds a coherent story from the information at hand and ignores what is missing. Confidence tracks story coherence, not evidence quality.
notes.extra: In practice: Three tidy options on a slide look complete. Ask: 'Which option is not on this slide, and why?'

notes.front: What is the substitution heuristic?
notes.back: Faced with a hard question, System 1 silently answers an easier related one. 'Is this vendor reliable?' becomes 'Do I like their sales engineer?'
notes.extra: In practice: 'Should we adopt this platform?' becomes 'Do I trust the person proposing it?' Put the real decision criteria on paper.

notes.front: What is the halo effect?
notes.back: One positive attribute (polish, reputation, likeability) colours judgement of unrelated attributes.
notes.extra: In practice: A vendor with a brilliant conference talk is assumed to have brilliant support. Score each evaluation dimension separately.

notes.front: What is status quo bias, and how does it interact with loss aversion?
notes.back: A preference for the current state, because any change is scored as gains and losses relative to now, and losses weigh more. The default wins unless the alternative is clearly better.
notes.extra: In practice: Migration proposals lose by default. Price the status quo as an active choice: 'Staying costs €X/yr and hits end-of-support in 2028.'

notes.front: What is loss aversion, and roughly how strong is it?
notes.back: Losses loom larger than equal gains, roughly 2:1 in experiments. People take risks to avoid a loss that they would not take to secure a gain.
notes.extra: In practice: 'We are losing €300k a year in duplicated infrastructure' moves executives more than 'this could save €300k'.

notes.front: What is the framing effect?
notes.back: Logically equivalent descriptions lead to different decisions depending on presentation: gain vs loss, percentage vs frequency, relative vs absolute.
notes.extra: In practice: '99.5% availability' sounds excellent; '44 hours of downtime a year' starts a different conversation. Choose the frame consciously and be ready to defend it.

notes.front: What is the sunk cost fallacy, and what question breaks it?
notes.back:
Continuing because of resources already spent, although only future costs and benefits matter.
Ask: 'If we started from zero today, knowing what we know, would we choose this?'
notes.extra: In practice: 'We spent €2M on the in-house orchestrator.' Reframe: the €2M is gone either way; is the next €500k better spent maintaining it or replacing it? (Also called the Concorde fallacy.)

notes.front: What is the overconfidence effect, and where is it strongest?
notes.back: Subjective confidence exceeds actual accuracy. Strongest on hard questions, for experts in their own domain, and when a coherent story is available.
notes.extra: In practice: Most engineers' '90% confidence intervals' contain the true value less than half the time. Widen intervals before they reach the board.

notes.front: What is the affect heuristic?
notes.back: Judging by feeling: things we like seem low-risk and high-benefit; things we dislike seem the reverse.
notes.extra: In practice: Executives who 'hate' a legacy system overrate every risk of keeping it. Score risk and benefit as separate dimensions.

notes.front: What is the narrative fallacy?
notes.back: Weaving facts into a causal story, then believing the story more than the facts warrant.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Adoption failed because the docs were bad' is a story. Check whether teams with good docs also failed to adopt.

notes.front: How does noise differ from bias in judgement?
notes.back:
Bias: systematic error in one direction.
Noise: unwanted variability: the same case gets different answers from different people, or from one person on different days.
notes.analogy: Bias is a rifle whose sight is off: tight group, wrong place. Noise is a shaky hand: shots scattered all over.
notes.extra: In practice: Five architects estimate one migration at 4 to 18 months. Reduce noise: independent estimates first, then aggregate, then discuss.

notes.front: What is regression to the mean, and why does it mislead managers?
notes.back: Extreme measurements tend to be followed by less extreme ones by chance alone, so managers credit interventions for improvements that would have happened anyway.
notes.extra: In practice: After a terrible incident quarter any change 'works'. Compare against the long-run average and a control, not the worst quarter.

notes.front: What is the planning fallacy, and why does it happen?
notes.back: Systematically underestimating time, cost and risk (and overestimating benefits), because plans are built as a story from the inside, case by case.

notes.front: What is the outside view, and why is it the remedy for the planning fallacy?
notes.back: Set the specifics aside and ask what happened to similar projects (a reference class). It replaces your story with a distribution of real outcomes.
notes.analogy: Instead of asking how fast you think you will drive, look at how long the trip took everyone else last week.
notes.extra: In practice: Inside: 'Our migration is 6 months.' Outside: 'The last five migrations of this size here took a median of 14 months.'

notes.text: Reference class forecasting: (1) identify a {{c1::reference class of comparable past projects}}, (2) establish the {{c2::distribution of outcomes}} in that class, (3) place the project in it and {{c3::adjust only for specific, defensible differences}}.
notes.extra: In practice: Use prior actual-vs-forecast ratios for cloud cost estimates and present a range ('50th percentile (P50) €1.2M, 90th percentile (P90) €1.9M').

notes.front: What is calibration, and how is it measured?
notes.back: When you say 70%, you are right about 70% of the time. Measured by comparing stated confidence with realised frequency over many predictions, scored with the Brier score.
notes.extra: In practice: Engineers tend to be overconfident on timelines. A prediction log of 50 entries shows your own bias before it reaches the steering committee.

notes.text: Brier score for a binary event = {{c1::(forecast probability − outcome)²}}, outcome 1 or 0. Lower is better: always saying 50% scores {{c2::0.25}}; a perfect forecaster scores {{c3::0}}.
notes.extra: In practice: Score architecture bets such as 'P(vendor X still supported in 3 years) = 0.9'.

notes.front: Why is calibration rare among engineers, and why does it matter for an architect's credibility?
notes.back: Engineers rarely get scored feedback on probabilistic claims: estimates are single numbers and misses get blamed on circumstances. Uncalibrated confidence costs credibility after the first missed date.
notes.extra: In practice: Say 'I'm 70% confident this fits Q4; the main risk is identity integration' instead of 'Q4'.

notes.front: Tetlock: what do superforecasters do differently?
notes.back:
• Use granular probabilities (63%, not 'likely')
  • Start from the outside view, then adjust
  • Decompose the question into parts
  • Update often, in small steps
notes.extra: In practice: Build vs buy: estimate P(team keeps key people), P(vendor raises price >30%) and so on, then revise as facts arrive instead of defending the first position.

notes.front: Tetlock: foxes vs hedgehogs: which forecast better, and why?
notes.back: Hedgehogs know one big thing and fit the world to it; foxes know many small things and aggregate diverse, independent views ('dragonfly eye'). Foxes forecast markedly better; hedgehogs are more quotable.
notes.extra: In practice: The architect who explains every problem as 'microservices' is a hedgehog. Collect independent views from security, finance, product and ops before converging.

notes.front: What is Fermi decomposition, and why does it improve estimates?
notes.back: Break an unknown quantity into sub-quantities you can estimate, then multiply. Errors partly cancel, and it exposes which assumption dominates. Aim for the right order of magnitude first.
notes.extra: In practice: Egress cost = users × sessions/day × MB/session × €/GB. A chief financial officer (CFO) can challenge one assumption instead of rejecting the whole number.

notes.front: Why does a premortem surface more risks than a normal risk review?
notes.back: Everyone assumes the project has already failed and writes why. This legitimises dissent, surfaces risks people would not raise as objections, and counters overconfidence.
notes.extra: In practice: 'It is 12 months from now and adoption is 10%. Why?' Executives hear risks as foresight, not negativity.

notes.front: How do you present expected value to executives without hiding the tails?
notes.back: EV = Σ probability × outcome. Present it as scenarios (best / expected / worst, with probabilities), because executives care about the downside, not only the mean.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Expected saving €800k, but a 15% chance we spend €300k extra on data-residency rework.'

notes.front: What is 'resulting', and why is it a mistake?
notes.back: Judging a decision by its outcome. A good decision is the best choice given the information and odds at the time; outcomes also depend on luck, so resulting teaches the wrong lessons.
notes.analogy: A poker player who goes all-in on a bad hand and wins still made a bad bet.
notes.extra: In practice: A risky cut-over that succeeded does not prove the risk was acceptable. Keep decision logs with stated probabilities so reviews judge the reasoning.

notes.front: How do you communicate uncertainty to the C-suite without sounding weak?
notes.back: Give a point estimate, a range, the main driver of the range, and what would narrow it. Structured uncertainty signals competence; vague hedging signals the opposite.
notes.extra: In practice: 'We expect €1.4M, range €1.1–2.0M, driven by the number of legacy integrations. Two weeks of discovery narrows it to ±15%.'

notes.front: What is a prediction log, and what gap in architecture work does it fill?
notes.back: A record of specific, dated, probabilistic predictions with resolution dates and outcomes. It supplies the fast, unambiguous feedback that architecture decisions normally lack.
notes.extra: Example: '75% that the identity migration passes security review by 30 Nov.' Review monthly; after 30–50 entries compute your Brier score.

notes.front: Systems thinking: what are stocks and flows, and why can't you change a stock instantly?
notes.back: A stock is an accumulation you can count at a moment; flows are the rates that fill or drain it. You can only change the flows, so stocks change slowly and create delays.
notes.analogy: A bathtub: you can't set the water level, only open the tap or the drain.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Teams on the platform' is a stock; onboarding and churn are flows. 50 teams in a year implies an onboarding rate: can the enabling team sustain it?

notes.front: Reinforcing vs balancing feedback loops: what does each do? Give a platform example.
notes.back:
Reinforcing: change amplifies itself (more teams → better docs → more teams).
Balancing: pushes back toward a goal or limit (more teams → longer support queue → slower onboarding).
notes.extra: In practice: Adoption plans that show only the reinforcing loop fail when the balancing loop (support capacity) kicks in.

notes.front: Why do delays in feedback loops cause oscillation and overshoot?
notes.back: When an action's effect shows up late, people keep pushing (or keep waiting) past the right point, then overcorrect.
notes.analogy: Adjusting the shower when hot water takes 30 seconds to arrive: scalded, then frozen.
notes.extra: In practice: Hiring platform engineers against last quarter's backlog: by the time they are productive the backlog has changed. Use leading indicators.

notes.text: Meadows' leverage points, weakest to strongest (selected): {{c1::parameters (numbers, budgets)}} < buffers < feedback strength < information flows < {{c2::rules of the system}} < self-organisation < {{c3::goals of the system}} < {{c4::paradigm / mindset}}.
notes.extra: In practice: Raising the platform budget is weak. The rule 'every new service has an owner and uses the golden path' is stronger. Changing the goal to 'ship safely at low marginal cost' is stronger still.

notes.front: What is policy resistance?
notes.back: Several actors with different goals each pull the system toward their own goal, so any policy change gets counteracted and the system stays stuck.
notes.extra: In practice: Mandating the platform while product is measured on velocity and ops on stability produces quiet non-compliance. Align the goals first.

notes.front: Describe the 'fixes that fail' archetype.
notes.back: A quick fix relieves a symptom but has an unintended consequence that worsens the underlying problem over time, so more of the fix is needed.
notes.extra: In practice: Granting teams cluster-admin to 'unblock' them creates security debt that later blocks everyone. Say so before the exception is granted.

notes.front: Describe the 'shifting the burden' archetype.
notes.back: A symptomatic solution is used instead of a fundamental one, and it weakens the capacity to apply the fundamental one, creating dependency.
notes.extra: In practice: A central team deploys for product teams instead of building self-service: teams never learn, the central team becomes the bottleneck, the platform never gets built.

notes.front: 'Fixes that fail' vs 'shifting the burden': what is the key difference?
notes.back:
Fixes that fail: the fix's side effect makes the original problem worse.
Shifting the burden: the fix erodes the ability to apply the real solution, creating dependency.

notes.front: Describe the 'limits to growth' archetype and the right response.
notes.back: A reinforcing growth loop eventually hits a balancing constraint. Pushing harder on growth does not help; you must remove the constraint.
notes.extra: In practice: Adoption grows until onboarding support saturates; marketing the platform harder then only adds frustration. Present the constraint and its removal cost.

notes.front: Theory of Constraints: what happens if you optimise something that is not the constraint?
notes.back: System throughput does not improve, and may get worse, because more work-in-progress piles up in front of the bottleneck.
notes.analogy: Widening the motorway before a one-lane bridge just makes a bigger traffic jam at the bridge.
notes.extra: In practice: Faster CI/CD pipelines do nothing if every change waits three weeks for a Change Advisory Board. Show the value stream with queue times.

notes.front: What is a mental model in Senge's sense, and why does it matter for platform adoption?
notes.back: A deeply held internal image of how the world works that shapes how people act. Change fails when it collides with unexamined mental models.
notes.extra: In practice: If ops believes 'developers can't be trusted with production', no tooling produces self-service. Surface the belief before proposing tools.

notes.front: What is the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre?
notes.back: Deliberately reshape teams and their communication paths to produce the architecture you want, instead of fighting the architecture the current org produces.
notes.extra: In practice: 'The target architecture won't happen while the platform team reports into infra ops and product teams into business units. Change the reporting lines first.'

notes.front: What is team cognitive load, and why is it the core argument for an internal platform?
notes.back: The total mental effort a team must spend. A platform exists to remove extraneous load (infrastructure, compliance, plumbing) so teams spend their capacity on the product.
notes.extra: In practice: Frame the business case as capacity: 'Each product team spends ~30% of engineering time on infrastructure; the platform returns that to feature work.'

notes.front: What is a sociotechnical system, and why is platform adoption a sociotechnical problem first?
notes.back: Technical and social subsystems are interdependent and must be designed together. Adoption depends on incentives, team boundaries, funding and trust, so a great platform can still fail.
notes.extra: In practice: Order a C-suite proposal: who owns and funds it → what changes in team incentives → which teams pilot → then the technology.

notes.front: State Goodhart's Law, with an adoption-metric example.
notes.back: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure: people optimise the number, not the outcome.
notes.extra: In practice: Target 'services on the platform' and teams register empty services. Prefer outcome measures: lead time, change failure rate, time-to-first-deploy.

notes.text: Westrum's organisational cultures: {{c1::pathological}} (power-oriented, information hoarded), {{c2::bureaucratic}} (rule-oriented, information may be ignored), {{c3::generative}} (performance-oriented, information sought). DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) research links {{c3::generative}} culture to higher delivery performance.
notes.extra: In practice: The vocabulary makes 'culture' discussable with executives when they ask why adoption worked elsewhere and not here.

notes.front: What are bounded rationality and satisficing?
notes.back: Decision-makers have limited information, time and attention, so they satisfice: they pick the first option that is good enough rather than optimising.
notes.extra: In practice: Executives won't read a 40-page comparison. Give a decision that is good enough on their criteria, on one page, with an appendix.

notes.text: Larman's Laws: (1) organisations are implicitly optimised to {{c1::avoid changing the status quo of middle-manager and specialist positions and power structures}}; (2) so any change initiative gets reduced to {{c2::relabelling the new terminology to mean the status quo}}.
notes.extra: In practice: 'We already do platform engineering': the ops team was renamed. Define the observable behaviours that would differ, not the labels.

notes.front: State Brooks's Law, and why it holds.
notes.back: Adding people to a late software project makes it later, because of ramp-up time and the growth of communication paths: n(n−1)/2.
notes.analogy: Nine women can't make a baby in one month.
notes.extra: In practice: When an executive proposes doubling the team to hit a date, show the onboarding cost and offer scope reduction instead.

notes.front: Why does a golden path (paved road) work better than a mandate, in systems terms?
notes.back: It changes the default: the desired behaviour becomes the path of least resistance (a rule-level intervention), so people choose it without enforcement.
notes.analogy: Paths across a lawn: pave where people want to walk and they stop cutting across the grass.
notes.extra: In practice: 'You can go off-road, but then you own compliance, on-call and cost. On the paved road the platform owns them.' That is an incentive structure, not a policy.

notes.front: Why is 'platform as a product' more than a slogan?
notes.back: It implies a product owner, user research, a demand-driven roadmap, adoption metrics, and the possibility of being ignored. Without these a platform is a mandated shared service that teams route around.
notes.extra: In practice: Ask the C-suite for a product owner and a funding model, not just headcount. Adoption is voluntary in practice even when mandatory on paper.

notes.front: What is Wardley mapping used for in an architecture decision?
notes.back: Placing components by visibility to the user (value chain) against evolution (genesis → custom → product → commodity) to decide what to build, buy or outsource.
notes.extra: In practice: Show that Kubernetes and identity are commodities (consume) while your domain orchestration layer is custom (build). It ends 'let's build a cloud' arguments.

notes.front: Stated vs revealed risk appetite: which governs decisions?
notes.back: Stated: what strategy documents say ('cloud-first', 'innovative'). Revealed: what leaders actually approve and punish. Revealed appetite governs.
notes.extra: In practice: If every exception request last year was denied, don't propose a plan that relies on exceptions, whatever the strategy slide says.

notes.text: Cialdini's seven principles of influence: {{c1::reciprocity}}, {{c2::commitment and consistency}}, {{c3::social proof}}, {{c4::authority}}, {{c5::liking}}, {{c6::scarcity}}, {{c7::unity}}.
notes.extra: In practice: Most architects lean on authority (expertise) alone, the weakest lever with executives who have their own experts.

notes.front: How does reciprocity work, and how does an architect use it ethically?
notes.back: People feel obliged to return favours, concessions and information. Ethical use: give real value first, such as a useful analysis or help with a problem that isn't yours.
notes.extra: In practice: Fix a product team's deployment pain before asking them to pilot the platform.

notes.front: How do you use commitment and consistency in a decision process?
notes.back: People act consistently with prior public commitments, especially written and voluntary ones. Secure small, explicit agreements early and build on them.
notes.extra: In practice: Get the steering committee to agree decision criteria in writing before presenting options; the option that meets their own criteria is hard to reject.

notes.front: What is the key condition for social proof to persuade?
notes.back: Similarity: people copy others like themselves, especially under uncertainty.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Three companies in our sector, including our main competitor, run this pattern' beats any benchmark. Internally: 'Team X halved its release time.'

notes.front: What is the weakness of the authority principle with executives?
notes.back: Executives are surrounded by experts with conflicting views, so unbacked authority gets discounted and can trigger reactance.
notes.extra: In practice: Borrow authority selectively (analysts, auditors, regulators) for claims executives can't evaluate; let your calibration track record carry the rest.

notes.front: How does liking work as an influence principle?
notes.back: People say yes more readily to people they like: similarity, genuine compliments, cooperation toward shared goals, and familiarity all increase liking.
notes.extra: In practice: Spend time with the ops lead on their problems before the proposal; a familiar collaborator is heard differently from a visiting architect.

notes.front: How do you use scarcity without manipulation?
notes.back: Limited availability or a deadline raises perceived value. Use only real ones: end-of-support dates, budget windows, regulatory deadlines.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Vendor end-of-life is Q2 2028; after that each month costs €40k in extended support.' Never invent urgency: executives remember.

notes.front: What is the unity principle, and how is it stronger than liking?
notes.back: Shared identity ('we', not 'us and them') raises influence far beyond liking: shared profession, region, mission or opponent.
notes.extra: In practice: Frame the platform as 'our engineering organisation's capability', and co-author the proposal with a product leader.

notes.front: What is pre-suasion?
notes.back: Arranging attention and context before the message so the audience is already receptive: what is salient at the moment of decision shapes the decision.
notes.extra: In practice: Open the board update with the incident-cost trend before asking for the reliability investment.

notes.text: Aristotle's modes of persuasion: {{c1::ethos}} (credibility of the speaker), {{c2::pathos}} (emotion of the audience), {{c3::logos}} (logic of the argument). Engineers over-invest in {{c3::logos}}.
notes.extra: In practice: A 100%-logos board deck loses to a 30-second story about a customer outage. Lead with the story, back it with numbers.

notes.front: What is steelmanning, and why does it persuade executives?
notes.back: Stating the strongest version of the opposing view before rebutting it. It shows you understand the trade-offs and are not selling.
notes.extra: In practice: 'The strongest case for staying on-prem is data residency and the sunk lease. Here's why I still recommend moving, and what would change my mind.'

notes.front: Why is architecture largely 'getting people to agree', and what follows?
notes.back: An architecture that isn't adopted doesn't exist, and decisions are made by people with interests and biases. So persuasion, stakeholder mapping and negotiation are core architecture work, not soft extras.
notes.extra: In practice: Put stakeholder interviews, pre-wiring and one-page memos on the plan explicitly.

notes.front: What is Hohpe's architect elevator?
notes.back: The architect rides between the penthouse (strategy, C-suite) and the engine room (implementation), translating in both directions so the two don't disconnect.
notes.extra: In practice: Translate 'we need a service mesh' into 'each security audit costs €X less and partner integrations take days, not weeks'.

notes.front: What is pre-wiring a decision?
notes.back: Meeting each decision-maker one-to-one before the group meeting to hear objections, adapt, and secure support, so the meeting ratifies rather than debates.
notes.extra: In practice: The steering committee should never see the proposal for the first time in the steering committee.

notes.front: What is disagree and commit, and when should an architect use it?
notes.back: Argue your position fully; once decided, support the decision without relitigating. Use it when you were heard and the decision is reversible or not catastrophic.
notes.extra: In practice: 'I still think X, and I'll make Y work. Here's how we'll know by Q2 if I was right.' It preserves credibility for the next decision.

notes.front: What is tactical empathy (Voss)?
notes.back: Deliberately understanding and articulating the counterpart's perspective and emotions so they feel understood, which is the precondition for them to hear you.
notes.extra: In practice: Before pushing back on a cost cut: 'It sounds like you're under real pressure to show a lower run-rate this year.'

notes.front: What is labelling (Voss), and what is its format?
notes.back: Naming the other side's emotion or position: 'It seems like…', 'It sounds like…'. Never 'I think you feel…'. Then stay silent.
notes.extra: In practice: 'It seems like there's concern this becomes another shelfware project.' They confirm (now address it) or correct you (now you know the real concern).

notes.front: What is mirroring (Voss)?
notes.back: Repeating the last one to three words the other person said, as a question, then staying silent. It prompts elaboration and signals attention.
notes.extra: In practice: 'We can't afford another failed platform.' → 'Another failed platform?' They then describe exactly what failure looked like last time.

notes.front: Labelling vs mirroring (Voss): what does each do?
notes.back:
Labelling names their emotion or position ('It sounds like…') to defuse it or confirm it.
Mirroring repeats their last words to get them to say more.

notes.front: What is an accusation audit?
notes.back: Listing up front every negative thing the other side might think about you or your proposal, before they say it. It defuses objections and shows you understand them.
notes.extra: In practice: 'You're probably thinking: third platform initiative in five years, the last two failed, same team asking for money.' Then explain what is different.

notes.front: What is a calibrated question, and why does it work?
notes.back: An open 'how' or 'what' question that makes the other side work on your problem while feeling in control: 'How am I supposed to do that?'
notes.extra: In practice: Faced with an impossible date: 'How do you see us doing this with the current compliance process?' They discover the constraint themselves.

notes.front: Why does Voss prefer 'no'-oriented questions?
notes.back: Saying 'no' makes people feel safe and in control; a 'yes' extracted early feels like a trap. 'Would it be a bad idea to…?' invites engagement without commitment.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Would it be a mistake to pilot with just two teams first?'

notes.front: 'That's right' vs 'you're right': what does each signal?
notes.back:
'That's right': they feel fully understood: a breakthrough.
'You're right': a polite way to end a conversation they want out of, so you have dismissal, not buy-in.
notes.extra: In practice: Summarise the executive's position until you hear 'that's right'.

notes.front: What are black swans in negotiation (Voss)?
notes.back: Unknown unknowns: facts that, once discovered, change the negotiation entirely. Found by listening, not pitching.
notes.extra: In practice: The chief financial officer (CFO) blocking the cloud budget may have a datacenter lease commitment you know nothing about. Ask before pitching.

notes.front: What is the Ackerman bargaining method?
notes.back: Set a target; open at 65% of it, then concede to 85%, 95%, 100% in shrinking steps; end on a precise, non-round number.
notes.extra: In practice: Vendor licence talks: shrinking concessions signal you're near your limit; €387,400 signals calculation, not haggling.

notes.front: Principled negotiation: what does 'separate the people from the problem' mean?
notes.back: Deal with relationship and emotion issues directly and separately from the substance: soft on the people, hard on the problem.
notes.extra: In practice: The ops lead blocking self-service is protecting their team's relevance. Discuss their role in the new model as its own conversation.

notes.front: Positions vs interests: what is the difference, and why does it matter?
notes.back: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it. Positions conflict; interests can often be reconciled.
notes.analogy: Two people fight over one orange; one wants the juice, the other the peel for baking. Ask why, and both get everything.
notes.extra: In practice: Position: 'Security approves every deployment.' Interest: auditability. Policy-as-code with an audit trail meets the interest without the position.

notes.front: What is a BATNA, and why is it the real source of negotiating power?
notes.back: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you do if talks fail. The side with the better walk-away option gets the better deal, not the side with better arguments.
notes.extra: In practice: Before a cloud renewal, have a credible, costed migration plan to a second provider, built before the negotiation starts.

notes.front: What does 'insist on objective criteria' mean?
notes.back: Base agreement on independent standards (market rates, benchmarks, regulation, precedent) rather than on will or pressure.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Benchmarks put platform teams at one engineer per 8–12 product teams; we have one per 25.' The number argues for you.

notes.front: What does 'invent options for mutual gain' mean?
notes.back: Separate inventing from deciding: generate many options before choosing, and look for interests valued differently that allow trades.
notes.extra: In practice: Chief financial officer (CFO) wants lower capex, you want flexibility: consumption pricing with a committed-use discount serves both.

notes.front: How do you handle a hostile question, from an executive or from an audience?
notes.back: Pause; restate or label it neutrally ('It sounds like the concern is…'); answer the concern, not the phrasing; concede the valid part. If you don't know, commit to a date for the answer.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Why would we trust this team with another €2M?' → 'It sounds like the last initiative's outcome is the real question.' Defend the reasoning, not your ego.

notes.front: What is the Pyramid Principle (Minto), and why does it suit executives?
notes.back: Answer first, then grouped supporting arguments, then data. The reader can stop at any level and still have the conclusion.
notes.analogy: A newspaper article: headline, then lead paragraph, then detail. Most readers stop early and still get the story.
notes.extra: In practice: Slide 1: 'Recommendation: managed Kubernetes on provider X; €1.2M over 3 years; decision needed by 30 Oct.' Everything after is support.

notes.front: How do you structure a one-page decision memo for the C-suite?
notes.back: Decision requested and by when; recommendation and cost; 2–3 options with cost, risk and time, including 'do nothing'; risks; next steps with owners. Detail goes in an appendix.
notes.extra: In practice: Executives choose between options; they don't design solutions. Pricing 'do nothing' stops the status quo looking free.

notes.front: What does a good BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) contain?
notes.back: The first sentence states the recommendation, its cost and ideally the key number. The reader could stop there and know what you want.
notes.extra: Example: Bad: 'This memo explores options for our upgrade process.' Good: 'Recommend automated weekly upgrades for non-prod at 0.5 full-time equivalent (FTE) from March; this removes our 3-week prod lag.'

notes.front: What is the 'so what' test?
notes.back: For every fact in an executive communication, ask what it implies for the decision. If there is no implication, cut it.
notes.extra: Example: 'The cluster runs 1.31': so what? 'The cluster leaves support in March, after which our cyber-insurance excludes it': decision-relevant.

notes.front: What belongs in an Architecture Decision Record's (ADR's) Context section, and what does not?
notes.back: Forces, constraints and facts that hold whichever option wins. No opinions or solution language: a reader should be able to reconstruct the world before the decision.
notes.extra: Example: 'Ingress API is frozen; 40 namespaces carry 200+ vendor annotations; cross-namespace routing needed.' Not: 'Gateway API is clearly better.'

notes.front: How do an Architecture Decision Record's (ADR's) Decision and Consequences sections differ?
notes.back:
Decision: one imperative sentence, 'We will…'.
Consequences: every result, positive and negative, including new work created. No downsides means marketing, not an ADR.
notes.extra: Example: 'One cluster per environment per region': better blast-radius isolation; more per-cluster overhead; we now need a fleet manager; tenants lose cluster-admin.

notes.front: Why record rejected alternatives in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)?
notes.back: It stops the decision being relitigated each time someone new joins or a vendor visits. The rejection reasons are often more valuable than the choice.
notes.extra: Example: 'Rejected the cloud container network interface (CNI): per-pod IPs exhaust our /24 subnets at ~200 pods per node.' Six months later, 'why not the default CNI?' has an answer in Git.

notes.front: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) status: when is it Superseded rather than Deprecated?
notes.back:
Superseded: a newer ADR replaces it (link both ways).
Deprecated: the decision no longer applies and nothing replaces it.
notes.extra: Example: 'Helm-only deployments' superseded by 'Kustomize + Argo CD'; 'Jenkins on the cluster' deprecated once CI left platform scope.

notes.front: Why are accepted Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) treated as immutable?
notes.back: The record must show what was known and believed at the time; editing it destroys the reason it exists. Change comes through a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
notes.analogy: A lab notebook: you don't erase old entries, you add a dated correction.
notes.extra: Example: Rewriting 'etcd on local NVMe' as 'managed control planes' erases the latency and cost reasoning a later reader needs to judge whether the constraints still hold.

notes.front: What signals an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is too long or holds the wrong content?
notes.back: It contains implementation detail: Helm values, YAML, runbook steps. Those live in the repo or runbook and the ADR links to them. Target: readable in five minutes.

notes.front: Which platform decisions deserve an Architecture Decision Record (ADR), and which don't?
notes.back: ADR when it is hard to reverse, has cross-team impact, or someone will ask 'why' in a year. Not for reversible config, one-team choices or routine upgrades.
notes.extra: Example: ADR: container network interface (CNI), cluster topology, GitOps tool, secrets backend. No ADR: bumping the horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) default target from 70% to 75%.

notes.front: How is an Amazon-style six-page narrative written and read?
notes.back: Prose, no slides: goal, tenets, current state, lessons, proposal, FAQ, appendices. The meeting opens with 20–30 minutes of silent reading, then discussion.
notes.extra: Example: An internal developer platform (IDP) six-pager whose FAQ pre-answers 'Why not just give teams kubectl and RBAC?'

notes.front: What is the job of the FAQ in a narrative memo?
notes.back: To state the hardest objections in the author's own words, sharper than critics would, and answer them. It shows the proposal is stress-tested and moves the meeting past the obvious.
notes.extra: Example: 'Q: Doesn't namespace multi-tenancy give 90% of the isolation? A: Not for payments: shared kernel and etcd, and API-server noisy-neighbour latency we measured at 1.2s p99.'

notes.front: What are tenets in a narrative memo?
notes.back: Non-negotiable principles stated up front, used later in the document and meeting as tie-breakers for trade-offs.
notes.extra: Example: 'Paved road, not walled garden: tenants may leave the golden path, but they own on-call for what they build off it.'

notes.front: Three fixes that turn a hedged recommendation ('X might be a reasonable direction') into a decision?
notes.back: Decision first; imperative voice ('We will…'); rejected options with reasons.
notes.extra: Example: 'We will use External Secrets Operator backed by Vault. Sealed Secrets and SOPS were rejected: both keep ciphertext in Git and can't rotate credentials.'

notes.front: Why does structured writing outlast verbal influence for an architect?
notes.back: A document is asynchronous proof of thinking: it reaches people you'll never meet (executives, auditors, future hires) and can be cited for years. Verbal influence ends with the meeting.
notes.extra: Example: The author of the cluster-topology Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is still 'the multi-cluster person' two years later.

notes.front: Why is explaining a hard thing simply the visible proof of understanding?
notes.back: No one can inspect your understanding directly. Simplifying without loss is the only outward signal that you hold the whole model, not just the vocabulary.
notes.extra: Example: 'The scheduler is a loop: find pending pods, filter nodes that can't host them, score the rest, bind.'

notes.front: What are the steps of the Feynman technique?
notes.back: Explain the concept in plain language as if to a novice → notice where you stall or reach for jargon (that's the gap) → go back to the source for that gap → simplify again.
notes.extra: Example: You say 'kube-proxy programs iptables': stop. Can you say what that rule does to a packet? If not, read there.

notes.front: What is the ladder of abstraction, and how do you use it when teaching?
notes.back: Move deliberately between concrete and abstract: start concrete, rise to the principle, then descend to a different concrete case the principle now explains.
notes.extra: Example: A PR changes replicas 3 → 5 and Argo CD syncs → desired state in Git, reconciled continuously → someone runs kubectl edit and the drift is reverted.

notes.front: What is a good structure for a ten-minute teaching talk?
notes.back: Hook (a pain they felt) → one core idea → three examples → a diagram or demo → one thing to do on Monday. Don't cover a topic; uncover one idea.
notes.extra: Example: Hook: 'Your pods were evicted at 03:00 during the upgrade.' Idea: drains respect PodDisruptionBudgets. Monday: add a PDB to every multi-replica Deployment.

notes.front: What is the curse of knowledge, and how do you counter it?
notes.back: Once you know something you can't imagine not knowing it, so you skip steps the audience needs. Fix: start from the symptom the audience experiences, not the mechanism you know.
notes.analogy: Tapping a song's rhythm on a table: it's obvious to you because you hear the tune; the listener hears only knocks.
notes.extra: Example: Not 'just add a PodDisruptionBudget' but 'here's why your pods disappeared in pairs at 03:00'.

notes.front: Analogy vs model when teaching: how should you use both?
notes.back: An analogy gets the listener started, then breaks. Give the analogy, show exactly where it breaks, then give the real model. Never leave them with only the analogy.
notes.extra: Example: 'Namespaces are like folders' → but folders don't carry quotas, RBAC scope or policy selectors → a namespace is a scope for names plus a boundary for quota, access and policy.

notes.front: How do you explain a platform trade-off to finance and executives?
notes.back: Translate into their currency (cost, risk, speed): give the number, then the trade-off you're asking them to accept. No tool names.
notes.extra: Example: '60 clusters cost 240 engineer-hours a month; consolidating to 12 frees ~1.5 full-time equivalent (FTE) but concentrates blast radius, so we'd spend that on tenant isolation.'

notes.front: What is the one-sentence test before preparing a talk?
notes.back: If you can't state the talk as one sentence a listener could repeat to a colleague, you have a topic, not a talk.
notes.extra: Example: Passes: 'Tenants should never need to know what a node is.' Fails: 'An overview of our autoscaling improvements.'

notes.front: Why draw a request-path diagram live instead of showing slides full of YAML?
notes.back: An audience can read or listen, not both: YAML on screen means they stop listening. Drawing as you narrate makes picture and words arrive together; YAML goes in a linked repo.

notes.front: Why is teaching only the happy path a mistake?
notes.back: People understand a system through its failure modes; the happy path teaches syntax, not the model.
notes.extra: Example: Teaching the horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA): show a missing metric, unset resources.requests (utilisation can't be computed), and a fight with vertical pod autoscaler (VPA) on the same Deployment.

notes.front: Why is an internal brown-bag session a cheap career lever?
notes.back: Thirty minutes reaches dozens of engineers and leaves a recording and a document. Visibility compounds when the artefact is linkable, e.g. from a runbook.

notes.front: How do you pitch depth for a mixed audience (developers, security, management)?
notes.back: Layer it: the first minutes for everyone, the middle for practitioners, a final section flagged 'for those who run this'. Signpost the transitions.
notes.extra: Example: Image signing: (1) 'unsigned images are refused in prod'; (2) how cosign signs in CI; (3) admission policy and key rotation.

notes.front: What makes a decision meeting actually decide?
notes.back:
• Pre-read ≥48h ahead, options written out
  • The decision as a question with options and explicit criteria
  • A named decider (not a vote) and a timebox
  • Decision, owner and date written down before leaving
notes.extra: Example: 'Decide: do tenants get cluster-admin on dev? Options A/B/C. Decider: Head of Platform. 30 min. Criteria: blast radius, support load, velocity.'

notes.front: Why state decision rights (decide / consult / input / inform) at the start of a meeting?
notes.back: Otherwise everyone assumes they hold a veto. Naming roles turns objections into input rather than blockers.
notes.extra: Example: Pod Security 'restricted' by default: security consulted, app leads give input, platform lead decides, chief technology officer (CTO) informed.

notes.front: How do you run a disagree-and-commit close?
notes.back: After the decider decides, ask each dissenter: 'Can you commit to executing this, though you'd have chosen otherwise?' Record the answer. Commitment is to execution, not agreement.
notes.extra: Example: The network team preferred Calico; decision is Cilium. Their commitment: own the migration runbook and the first two cut-overs.

notes.front: Decision record vs meeting notes: what's the difference?
notes.back: Notes: what was said. Decision record: what was decided, by whom, why, which alternatives were rejected, and what would reopen it. Notes are disposable; the record feeds the Architecture Decision Record (ADR).
notes.extra: Example: 'Reopen if Cilium enterprise pricing exceeds €X/node/year or we need Windows nodes.'

notes.front: How do you fix a status meeting disguised as a decision meeting?
notes.back: If no one must choose between options with real trade-offs, cancel it or go async. Turn every agenda item into a question with options, or drop it.
notes.extra: Example: 'Review the upgrade plan' → 'Decide: prod upgrade in business hours via canary clusters (A) or a weekend window (B).'

notes.front: A stakeholder keeps blocking a platform change. How do you surface the real objection?
notes.back: Ask about consequences, not positions: 'What would have to be true for this to work for you?' The real objection is usually operational or political, not the technical argument.
notes.extra: Example: A team refusing Gateway API turned out to have no routing tests and a two-person on-call. The platform wrote the smoke test; the container network interface (CNI) debate was irrelevant.

notes.front: Stakeholder map for a Kubernetes platform: what does each of the four groups want?
notes.back:
• Tenant developers: speed, fewer foot-guns
  • App tech leads: predictability, control
  • Security / compliance: evidence, enforced policy
  • Leadership / finance: cost, risk, headcount
notes.extra: The same decision needs four one-liners. Example: image signing → devs: 'one CI step, template provided'; leadership: 'closes audit finding 4 at zero headcount'.

notes.front: How do you run a premortem for a cluster migration?
notes.back: Assume it's six months later and it failed. Everyone writes why, silently, for five minutes; cluster the answers; the top three become mitigations or decision criteria with owners.
notes.extra: Example: 'Stateful workloads on local volumes couldn't move'; 'DNS cut-over broke external clients'.

notes.front: How do you stop the loudest engineer deciding by volume?
notes.back: Silent writing first (everyone writes option and reasoning), round-robin reading, decider speaks last. Options on the board, so the argument is about artefacts, not people.

notes.front: What does a well-run escalation look like?
notes.back: Both parties escalate together with one shared page: agreed facts, the disagreement in one sentence, each option with the trade-off the other side cares about, and the decision needed.
notes.extra: Example: 'Both end in default-deny NetworkPolicy. Security wants it day one, platform wants 90 days observe-only. Decide the phase-in length.'

notes.front: What do you say in the last two minutes of every decision meeting?
notes.back: 'We decided X. Owner is Y. It's recorded at Z. Anyone who can't commit?' Then send the record within the hour, before memories diverge.

notes.front: A stakeholder agreed in the meeting but undermines the decision afterwards. What do you do?
notes.back: Go direct and private; cite the recorded commitment; ask what changed. If something material changed, reopen formally; if not, ask them to stop. Tolerated drift teaches that decisions are optional.

notes.front: How do you handle a decision when the decider isn't in the room?
notes.back: Don't fake it: produce a decision package (options, recommendation, recorded dissent, deadline). 'We'll check with X' is not a decision-ready artefact.
notes.extra: Example: 'Recommend B (canary clusters). Network lead prefers A. Decision needed by Friday to hit the upgrade window.'

notes.front: 'What problem is this platform solving?': what separates a bad answer from a good one?
notes.back: Bad: names the technology. Good: names the users, the pain and a measurable outcome. Kubernetes is the implementation, never the product.
notes.extra: Example: 'Cut merged-code-to-production for 30 teams from days to under an hour, with security controls applied by default.'

notes.front: What is a Job To Be Done (JTBD) for a platform user?
notes.back: 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so that [outcome].' It describes the user's goal, never a platform feature.
notes.analogy: People don't want a quarter-inch drill; they want a quarter-inch hole.
notes.extra: Example: 'When I have a new service, I want it in staging with logs, metrics and a URL, so I can demo it Thursday.' Not 'I want a namespace.'

notes.front: What are cheap user-research methods for a platform team?
notes.back:
• Watch a developer onboard a service without helping
  • 5–8 interviews: 'walk me through your last deploy'
  • Mine tickets and the help channel
  • Measure time-to-first-deploy
notes.extra: Example: Watching one onboarding revealed a hidden fifth step: asking in Slack which Helm chart version to use.

notes.front: Platform as a product vs as a mandate: how can you tell which you have?
notes.back: Product: teams adopt because it's better and adoption is tracked. Mandate: teams use it because they must. Signal: do teams ask you for features, or route around you?
notes.extra: Example: A team quietly running its own EKS cluster is the loudest possible research finding.

notes.front: How do you decide between two roadmap items (e.g. multi-cluster mesh vs self-service onboarding)?
notes.back: Against the problem statement and evidence, not interest. Write down what you are not doing and the condition under which you'd revisit.
notes.extra: Example: 20 teams wait three days for a namespace; two need cross-cluster mTLS. Onboarding wins; mesh deferred unless a third team needs it.

notes.front: What product decision does a golden path encode?
notes.back: Which ~80% of use cases you make excellent and fully supported, and that the other 20% get 'you can, but you own it'.
notes.extra: Example: Golden path: stateless HTTP service with Deployment, HTTPRoute, ServiceMonitor, pod disruption budget (PDB) and one values file. StatefulSets on local storage: allowed, unsupported.

notes.front: Which metrics measure the platform as a product, not cluster operations?
notes.back: Time-to-first-deploy, DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) lead time and deploy frequency, share of workloads on the golden path, tickets per deploy, and developer satisfaction.
notes.extra: Node CPU and etcd latency are operations metrics: necessary, but silent on whether tenants are better off.

notes.front: How do you say no to a feature request product-style (e.g. Windows nodes)?
notes.back: Understand the underlying job → quantify demand → name the full cost → offer an alternative → record it, so the next request starts from evidence.
notes.extra: Example: One team, one legacy .NET service; cost: separate node pool and image pipeline, half the ecosystem unsupported. Alternative: port to .NET 8 on Linux.

notes.front: What is the internal customer trap?
notes.back: Treating tenants as captive, so value is never validated and the platform team gets no honest feedback. Counter it by acting as if they could leave.
notes.extra: Example: Publish a service level objective (SLO), a roadmap and a deprecation policy; run office hours. If teams still stay, that's evidence.

notes.front: What does a good platform deprecation look like?
notes.back: Announce a date at least two release cycles out → provide a migration path and tooling → show each tenant what of theirs is affected → warn in-cluster → then enforce.
notes.extra: Silence until enforcement is the failure mode. Example: kubectl apply warnings for 60 days before rejecting old Ingress annotations.

notes.front: How do you make the opportunity cost of platform hygiene visible on the roadmap?
notes.back: Reserve a fixed share of capacity for upgrades, patching and toil, and put the rest on the public roadmap, so the split is a decision rather than a default.
notes.extra: Example: '30% reserved for hygiene. When the upgrade slipped, it came out of the 30%, not out of self-service onboarding.'

notes.front: What goes into a problem statement, before any solution is named?
notes.back: Who · what pain · evidence · what it costs · what 'solved' looks like. Only then name a tool.
notes.extra: Example: 'New services take four days to reach staging (11 onboardings measured) because of four separate tickets. Solved: under an hour, zero tickets.'

notes.front: Feature request vs problem report: why log the problem?
notes.back: A feature request is the user's proposed solution; a problem report is the pain. Log the pain, or the roadmap becomes a list of other people's designs.
notes.extra: Example: Request: 'cluster-admin on dev'. Problem: 'we can't install the operator's custom resource definitions (CRDs)'. Better fit: a self-service namespaced operator catalogue.

notes.front: What is the spacing effect?
notes.back: Learning is more durable when study is spread out over time than massed. A review near the point of forgetting strengthens memory more than one while it is fresh.
notes.extra: In practice: Spaced sessions over a month beat re-reading the provider's architecture guide the night before the exam.

notes.front: What is the testing effect (retrieval practice)?
notes.back: Actively retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than re-studying, even when retrieval fails, provided feedback follows.
notes.analogy: Memory is a path through a forest: each walk wears it deeper; reading the map doesn't.
notes.extra: In practice: Before a design review, write the trade-offs from memory, then check.

notes.front: What are desirable difficulties?
notes.back: Conditions that make learning feel slower and harder but improve long-term retention and transfer: spacing, interleaving, retrieval, generation, varied conditions.

notes.front: What is interleaving, and why does it beat blocked practice?
notes.back: Mixing problem types in one session instead of practising one type at a time. It forces you to choose which approach applies, which is what real problems demand.
notes.extra: In practice: Mix architecture katas across domains (payments, IoT, batch) instead of five payment systems in a row.

notes.text: Deliberate practice (Ericsson) requires a {{c1::specific goal}}, {{c2::full concentration}}, {{c3::immediate informative feedback}}, {{c4::repetition with refinement}}, and working {{c5::just beyond current ability}}. Mere experience doesn't qualify.
notes.extra: In practice: Twenty years of presenting isn't practice. Recording one presentation a month, scoring it against a rubric and fixing one thing is.

notes.front: Why does experience alone often fail to produce expertise?
notes.back: Without feedback and deliberate stretch, performance plateaus at 'acceptable' and becomes automatic. With noisy or delayed feedback, experience can even entrench wrong beliefs.
notes.extra: In practice: Architecture feedback takes years. Substitute faster loops: scored predictions, peer design reviews, post-implementation reviews at 6 and 12 months.

notes.front: Kahneman & Klein: when can expert intuition be trusted?
notes.back: Only when the environment is regular enough to have valid cues and the expert has had long practice with rapid, clear feedback. Otherwise intuition is confident but uninformative.
notes.extra: In practice: Trust a senior site reliability engineer's (SRE's) gut during an outage; distrust anyone's gut on five-year technology bets: use the outside view.

notes.front: Near vs far transfer: what is the difference, and what does far transfer need?
notes.back: Near: applying learning to closely similar situations. Far: to different domains or surface features. Far transfer is rare and needs the underlying principle, not just the case.
notes.extra: In practice: Knowing a Kubernetes control loop is a balancing feedback loop lets you spot the same structure in a hiring pipeline.

notes.front: What conditions promote transfer of learning?
notes.back: State the abstract principle explicitly; use several varied examples; compare cases to extract the shared structure; practise retrieval in new contexts.
notes.extra: In practice: Study anchoring with a vendor-pricing, a timeline and a salary example, then state the rule. One example gives a fact; three plus a rule give a tool.

notes.front: What is elaboration as a learning strategy?
notes.back: Explaining new material and connecting it to what you already know: asking how and why, and generating your own examples.
notes.extra: In practice: For each principle, write one example from your own last quarter.

notes.front: What is the generation effect?
notes.back: Information you produce yourself (answers, examples, solutions) is retained better than information you read or are given.
notes.extra: In practice: Sketch your own design before reading a reference architecture. Even when yours is wrong, the correction sticks.

notes.text: Cognitive load theory: {{c1::intrinsic}} load (complexity inherent to the material), {{c2::extraneous}} load (caused by poor presentation), {{c3::germane}} load (effort building schemas). Good instruction minimises {{c2::extraneous}} load.
notes.extra: In practice: A 60-box diagram in a C-suite deck is almost all extraneous load. Three boxes and one arrow per decision point.

notes.front: What is the expertise reversal effect?
notes.back: Support that helps novices (worked examples, step-by-step guidance) becomes redundant or harmful for experts, who learn better from solving problems.
notes.extra: In practice: Platform docs need both a 'first deploy in 10 minutes' path and a reference path.

notes.front: What is chunking, and how does it explain expertise?
notes.back: Grouping pieces of information into larger meaningful patterns held as one item in working memory. Experts see chunks where novices see pieces.
notes.analogy: A chess master sees 'castled king under attack'; a beginner sees 20 separate pieces.
notes.extra: In practice: A senior architect sees 'command query responsibility segregation (CQRS) with an outbox' where a junior sees twelve services. Named patterns are chunks, which is why shared vocabulary speeds reviews.

notes.front: What is the illusion of competence (fluency illusion)?
notes.back: Mistaking ease of processing (re-reading, highlighting, watching a demo) for understanding. Familiarity feels like knowledge.
notes.extra: In practice: A conference talk on event sourcing feels understood until you must design one. Test yourself before claiming the skill.

notes.front: What is metacognition, and why does calibrated self-assessment matter for learning?
notes.back: Monitoring and controlling your own thinking: knowing what you know. Calibrated learners spend time on what they don't know; uncalibrated ones re-study what feels fluent.
notes.extra: In practice: Cards where you were confident and wrong are where the study time should go.

notes.front: What is the minimum information principle for flashcards?
notes.back: Each card tests one atomic fact or relation. Complex cards are forgotten as a whole and can't be scheduled efficiently.
notes.extra: Example: 'Explain Cialdini' is a bad card; 'What is the key condition for social proof?' is a good one.

notes.front: How do spaced repetition algorithms choose the next review interval?
notes.back: They model each item's forgetting curve and schedule the review just before predicted recall drops below a target (e.g. 90%). Success lengthens the interval; failure shortens it.
notes.extra: In practice: Same for team knowledge: a runbook not exercised in 18 months is no longer known. Schedule game days at the edge of forgetting.

notes.front: Schema vs fact: which should you aim to memorise, and why?
notes.back: A fact is an isolated item; a schema is an organised structure of related concepts that lets you interpret new situations. Facts are useful mainly as anchors for schemas.
notes.extra: Example: 'Loss aversion ≈ 2:1' is a fact; 'reframe gains as avoided losses for the C-suite', with three examples, is a usable schema.

notes.front: What is dual coding?
notes.back: Combining verbal and visual representations of an idea improves retention, because they are stored and retrieved through partly independent channels.
notes.extra: In practice: Draw the causal-loop diagram when explaining 'limits to growth' to a chief information officer (CIO) rather than describing it.

notes.front: What is wrong with the popular '10,000-hour rule'?
notes.back: It is a popularisation. Ericsson's claim was that the amount of deliberate practice, not hours of experience, predicts expert performance, and the amount varies by domain.
notes.extra: In practice: Don't ask for 'experienced engineers'; specify what deliberate practice and feedback the role requires.
